analysis.one_liner: Requires federal health programs to fill prescriptions with cheaper generic drugs unless a doctor or patient requests brand-name.
analysis.headline: The bill died in the Senate committee where it was referred, with no cosponsors and no vote before the 106th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required federal health programs — Medicare, Medicaid, the Federal Employees Health Benefits program, the Indian Health Service, veterans' care, military health care, and prisons — to fill prescriptions with the generic version of a drug whenever one is available, unless the prescribing doctor or the patient specifically chose the brand-name version. It also would have required the FDA to formally determine, before approving a generic, that it works the same as the brand-name drug, and set a national standard for that judgment. The Congressional Budget Office figures cited in the bill estimated generics cost 25% to 60% less, saving $15 to $30 on an average prescription and $8 to $10 billion a year for drug purchasers.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients in federal health programs — Medicare and Medicaid beneficiaries, federal employees, veterans, service members, and people served by the Indian Health Service — would pay less out of pocket or through premiums as programs filled prescriptions with generics costing 25% to 60% less than brand-name drugs [S2][S3]. Taxpayers would also benefit, since the government funds most of these programs and the bill cited estimates of $8 to $10 billion in annual savings to purchasers [S3]. Generic drug makers would gain a larger, federally guaranteed market, backed by a new national FDA determination of therapeutic equivalence [S2][S3].

how_it_helps.text: Federal health programs would default to the generic form of a drug whenever feasible, with generic drugs costing 25% to 60% less and saving an estimated $15 to $30 per prescription, according to CBO figures cited in the bill.
The bill preserves choice: a doctor who specifically orders the brand-name version, or a patient who requests it, would still get it.

The FDA would have to determine, before approving a generic application, that the drug is therapeutically equivalent to its brand-name counterpart, giving prescribers and patients a national, uniform assurance the generic works the same.
The bill urged that a generic-drug preference be written into any Medicare prescription drug benefit Congress might add, so a new program would not start by paying brand-name prices.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers would lose sales in federal health programs, which together cover tens of millions of people, as prescriptions default to cheaper generics. The government itself would save an estimated $8 to $10 billion a year in reduced drug purchases, which is the drug makers' forgone revenue [S3].

drawbacks.text: Title II would supersede any state law on determining therapeutic equivalence, replacing state-level determinations with a single federal standard — a national uniformity provision that some states might view as removing a layer of local consumer protection.

Mandating generic substitution could reduce brand-name manufacturers' revenue from federal programs, and industry would argue that weaker returns on sales erode the incentive to develop new medicines, even though the bill lets doctors and patients opt out.

The enforcement language is soft — it requires generic substitution only 'to the extent feasible' — so savings depend heavily on how programs and carriers implement it, and Title III is merely a nonbinding statement of Senate opinion.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core idea is low-risk and potentially large in dollar terms: generic drugs are already FDA-approved equivalents costing far less, and the bill keeps patient and doctor choice intact with explicit exceptions. The main honest concerns are that the 'to the extent feasible' language makes the mandate soft, and that preempting state therapeutic-equivalence laws trades local rules for a single federal standard. Weighing those against $8-10 billion in annual purchaser savings, the bill's design favors consumers more than it burdens anyone else.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee on the day it was introduced, the committee never acted on it, and it died there when the 106th Congress ended in January 2001.

narrative.text: Sen. Tim Johnson introduced the bill on May 3, 2000, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee the same day.
No further action was recorded after the referral; the bill never received a committee vote or a Senate floor vote before the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug makers are better off: they kept federal health programs paying brand-name prices for drugs with available generic equivalents, and taxpayers and federal program beneficiaries continued absorbing the difference. The bill's failure also left the generic-preference question for a future Medicare drug benefit unanswered in 2000.

for.name: Tim Johnson
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the Senate floor on May 3, 2000.

against.name: Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.role: Committee of referral (chaired by James Jeffords, R-VT)
against.what_they_did: Never acted on the bill after referral; no markup, no committee vote, and no floor vote before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Democratic sponsor, zero cosponsors of either party, and never reached a vote, so the record shows no party split — only that no one else picked it up.

industries.note: Federal health programs covering Medicare, Medicaid, veterans, military, and federal employees would default to generics costing 25-60% less, cutting brand-name sales across tens of millions of patients — savings estimated at $8-10 billion a year for purchasers. Those savings are the industry's forgone revenue.

A national FDA determination of therapeutic equivalence and a federal substitution mandate would expand the generics market and preempt inconsistent state rules, giving generic makers a larger, federally standardized customer base. Their gain comes from the same mechanism that lowers drug costs for patients.
